title: 04. AsyncIO: Day 5 — Async Fundamentals: Event Loop & Coroutines

title: 04. AsyncIO: Day 7 — Async Synchronization Primitives

Build a bounded async DB connection pool.

title: 07. Python Internals: Topic 1 — Core Execution: How Python Runs Your Code
summary: Python is compiled, not interpreted line-by-line. When you run a .py file, CPython goes through four stages:
objectives: Trace the full compilation pipeline: source → tokens → AST → code objects → bytecode.
Inspect a code object's anatomy (co_code, co_consts, co_names, co_varnames).
Explain the eval loop (ceval.c) and how it walks the bytecode.
Describe the frame stack and how function calls push/pop frames.
Predict which bytecode each Python statement compiles to (dis.dis).
Explain name binding and the LEGB scoping rule at the bytecode level.

title: 07. Python Internals: Topic 2 — Object Model: PyObject, Types, Caches
summary: In CPython, every Python object — integers, strings, lists, functions, classes, modules, None — is a PyObject* in C. The C struct starts with two fields:
objectives: Explain that every Python object is a PyObject* in C with ob_refcnt and ob_type.
Describe the type system and why type is its own metaclass.
Predict when Python reuses objects via the small integer cache (-5 to 256) and string interning.
Distinguish identity (is) from equality (==) and know when each applies.
Use ctypes to inspect the raw memory of a PyObject.
Walk the MRO (Method Resolution Order) for multiple inheritance.

title: 07. Python Internals: Topic 3 — Dictionary Internals: From Hash Table to Compact Dict
summary: Before 3.6, a dict was a single large array of (hash, key, value) entries. To keep lookups fast (O(1)), the table had to be at most 2/3 full — the remaining 1/3 was empty slots to terminate probe sequences.
objectives: Describe the pre-3.6 sparse hash table layout and its memory waste.
Explain the compact dict design (3.6+) — two arrays: sparse indices + dense entries.
Predict why dicts maintain insertion order (and why it's guaranteed since 3.7+).
Describe Python's hash function (SipHash-1-3), hash randomization (PYTHONHASHSEED), and why it matters.
Walk through open addressing with the perturbation probe sequence used on collision.
Explain the 2/3 load-factor threshold and the resize algorithm.

title: 07. Python Internals: Topic 4 — Set Internals: A Dict Without Values
summary: A set is essentially a dict where you only care about the keys — the "value" slot is removed. All the hash table mechanics (compact layout, perturbation probe, 2/3 load factor, hash randomization) are identical to dict.
objectives: Explain that a set is a hash table with keys but no values — same memory layout as dict.
Describe why frozenset exists (hashable → can be a set member or dict key).
Predict the time complexity of set operations: in, union, intersection, difference, symmetric_difference.
Explain why sets require hashable elements (same as dict keys).
Use sets for deduplication, membership testing, and set algebra.
Decide between set, dict (when you need values), and list (when you need order + duplicates).

title: 07. Python Internals: Topic 5 — Memory Management: Refcount + GC + pymalloc
summary: For objects 512 bytes or smaller, CPython uses its own allocator:
objectives: Explain the three layers of CPython memory management: refcount, cyclic GC, and pymalloc.
Describe how Py_INCREF / Py_DECREF work and why refcounting is the primary mechanism.
Identify reference cycles and explain why refcounting alone can't collect them.
Describe the generational garbage collector (3 generations, threshold tuning).
Use the gc module to inspect, tune, and disable garbage collection.
Explain pymalloc's arena / pool / block architecture and the 512-byte threshold.

title: 07. Python Internals: Topic 6 — GIL Deep Dive: Mechanics, Tuning, and the nogil Future
summary: The Global Interpreter Lock is a single mutex (specifically a pthread_mutex_t or Windows critical section) defined in Python/ceval_gil.c. Every thread that wants to execute Python bytecode must hold this lock.
objectives: Explain what the GIL is, where it lives in CPython source, and why it exists.
Describe the eval breaker mechanism and sys.setswitchinterval (default 5ms).
Identify the exact conditions under which the GIL is released (I/O, C extensions, periodic check).
Predict when threading will and won't speed up Python code.
Explain why multiprocessing bypasses the GIL.
Use sys.setswitchinterval to tune GIL behavior for I/O-bound vs CPU-bound workloads.
